tagline: Free interactive chemistry simulations and practice for high school
home_title: Free Chemistry Simulations & Interactive Labs | ChemistryTeacher.net
home_description: Free interactive chemistry simulations for high school: gas laws, Lewis dot structures, naming compounds, heating curves, calorimetry, endothermic vs exothermic reactions, atoms, isotopes, alpha, beta and gamma radiation, a cloud chamber and nuclear equations. No login.
home_intro: Free, hands-on chemistry simulations built by a high school chemistry teacher for real classrooms. Every activity runs right in the browser on Chromebooks, laptops, tablets and classroom projectors. No logins, no ads, and no student data collected.
about_site: ChemistryTeacher.net is made by a high school chemistry teacher with about twenty years in the classroom. Each activity was built to fix a spot where students usually get stuck, then tested with real classes. Teachers are welcome to use every activity with their students for free. Please link to the page here instead of re-posting the files.
license: Free for classroom use. Please link to ChemistryTeacher.net rather than re-hosting.

dimensional-analysis.name: Dimensional Analysis Lab
dimensional-analysis.title: Dimensional Analysis Practice: Unit & Mole Conversions
dimensional-analysis.description: Free interactive dimensional analysis (factor-label) practice. Build conversion factors, cancel units and solve unit, mole and stoichiometry conversions step by step.
dimensional-analysis.card: Build conversion factors, cancel units, and solve unit, mole and stoichiometry problems.
dimensional-analysis.about: Dimensional analysis (the factor-label method) is the problem-solving tool students use all year, from metric conversions to stoichiometry. In this lab, students set up the starting amount, drag in conversion factors, and watch units cancel, so they see why a factor goes on top or bottom instead of memorizing it.
how: Choose Unit Conversion or Mole Conversion at the top.
Use Guided mode to practice 2-fraction and 3-fraction problems, or Free Form to set up your own.
Enter the starting amount, then add conversion factors so the unwanted units cancel.
Open the periodic table for molar masses in mole and stoichiometry (4-fraction) problems.
dimensional-analysis.classroom: Use it as a warm-up before a conversions quiz, on the projector to model setups, or as stoichiometry practice where students must show every factor.

atomic-theory.name: History of Atomic Theory
atomic-theory.title: History of Atomic Theory Timeline: Interactive Atomic Models
atomic-theory.description: Interactive history of atomic theory timeline: Democritus, Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr and the quantum model. Compare atomic models, then take a short quiz.
atomic-theory.card: Travel the timeline from Democritus to the quantum model, compare each atomic model, then take the quiz.
atomic-theory.about: The atomic model changed each time a new experiment did not fit the old one. This interactive timeline walks students through each major discovery, shows the model scientists used at that point, and lets them compare it side by side with the model before it, so they connect each change to the evidence that caused it.
how: Use Prev and Next to move through the 8 stops on the timeline.
Press Compare to previous model to see what changed and why.
View all 8 stops to unlock the quiz.
Finish the quiz to get a score card. No names or personal information are collected.
atomic-theory.classroom: Works well as a self-paced introduction to atomic structure, a station activity, or review before a unit test. The score card gives a quick completion check.

atom-builder.name: Atom Builder: Isotopes & Ions
atom-builder.title: Atom Builder: Protons, Neutrons, Electrons, Isotopes & Ions
atom-builder.description: Build an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons. Free interactive practice for isotopes, ions, mass number, atomic number, hyphen and nuclear notation.
atom-builder.card: Add protons, neutrons and electrons to build atoms, isotopes and ions, then name them in hyphen and nuclear notation.
atom-builder.about: Students build atoms by dragging protons, neutrons and electrons onto the model and see how each particle changes the element, the mass number, or the charge. Guided levels move from counting particles to building, naming and converting between hyphen notation and nuclear (isotope) notation.
how: Pick Free Form to explore, or Guided to work through 5 levels: Count It, Build It, Name It, Convert It and Mixed.
Drag particles onto the atom. Double-click a particle or drag it off to remove it.
Use the x1, x5 and x10 buttons to add particles faster.
Tap an answer box and use the keypad to enter numbers and charges.
atom-builder.classroom: Great for the first day of isotopes and ions, as a projector demo, or as practice before a quiz on subatomic particles.

types-of-radiation.name: Types of Radiation: Alpha, Beta & Gamma
types-of-radiation.title: Alpha, Beta & Gamma Radiation: Interactive Shielding Lab & Quiz
types-of-radiation.description: Free interactive lesson on alpha, beta and gamma radiation: penetrating vs ionizing power, shielding with paper, aluminum and lead, a Geiger counter lab, inverse-square law and quiz.
types-of-radiation.card: Compare alpha, beta and gamma radiation, then test shields and mystery sources with a virtual Geiger counter.
types-of-radiation.about: Students learn what alpha, beta and gamma radiation are, why ionizing and penetrating power are opposites, and how charged plates bend each type. In the Shielding Lab they block each source with skin, paper, wood, aluminum, lead or concrete and watch a Geiger counter (with real background radiation), then use those skills to identify mystery sources, including one that gives off both beta and gamma.
how: Work through the 8 Learn stops (Back/Next or tap a numbered stop).
In the Lab, choose a source and drag one shield into the slot. Readings record automatically.
Use the shields to identify the mystery sources.
When the Lab Checklist is done, take the 10-question quiz and download or email your score card.
types-of-radiation.classroom: Use it as notes and a virtual lab when you can't use real sources, as a pre-lab before a Geiger counter demo, or as review before a nuclear chemistry quiz. The score card can be turned in through Google Classroom or Gmail.

cloud-chamber.name: Cloud Chamber Simulator
cloud-chamber.title: Cloud Chamber Simulator: See Alpha, Beta, Gamma & Muon Tracks
cloud-chamber.description: Free interactive cloud chamber: watch alpha, beta, gamma-electron and cosmic-ray muon tracks form in alcohol vapor. Real sources, shields, magnetic field and quiz.
cloud-chamber.card: Watch alpha, beta and muon tracks form in a virtual cloud chamber, test shields and a magnet, then identify tracks in a game.
cloud-chamber.about: Students learn how a diffusion cloud chamber works: dry ice chills alcohol vapor until it is supersaturated, and charged particles leave trails of droplets. In the Lab they watch realistic tracks from a smoke-detector source, a thorium lantern mantle, uranium glass and sealed Sr-90, Cs-137, Co-60 and Po-210 sources, block them with paper, aluminum or lead, bend them with a magnetic field, and name tracks in a Track-ID game.
how: Work through the 8 Learn stops (Back/Next or tap a numbered stop).
In the Lab, choose a source, then try each shield and the magnetic field. The Lab Checklist ticks itself off.
Play the Track-ID Game: name 10 tracks and score 8 or more.
Then take the 10-question quiz and download or email your score card.
cloud-chamber.classroom: Use it before or alongside a real cloud chamber demo, when you don't have dry ice or sources, or as review for nuclear chemistry. The score card can be turned in through Google Classroom or Gmail.

nuclear-equations.name: Nuclear Equation Builder
nuclear-equations.title: Nuclear Equation Builder: Alpha, Beta, Gamma Decay Practice
nuclear-equations.description: Free interactive practice balancing nuclear equations: alpha decay, beta decay, positron emission, gamma radiation, fission and fusion. Check mass and atomic numbers.
nuclear-equations.card: Balance nuclear equations for alpha, beta, positron and gamma decay by matching mass and atomic numbers.
nuclear-equations.about: Balancing a nuclear equation comes down to one rule: the mass numbers and the atomic numbers must add up the same on both sides. Students build each side from particles like alpha, beta, positron, proton, neutron and gamma, and the builder checks the top (A) and bottom (Z) totals for them.
how: Choose Guided (Levels 1 to 3) or Free Form.
Tap a species to edit it, and tap its symbol to change the element.
Add particles from the palette to the left or right side.
Press Check to test your equation, or Hint if you are stuck.
nuclear-equations.classroom: Use it after introducing types of radioactive decay, as guided practice before a nuclear chemistry quiz, or for students to check their paper work.

lewis-dot-structures.name: Lewis Dot Builder
lewis-dot-structures.title: Lewis Dot Structure Builder: Covalent & Ionic Bonding
lewis-dot-structures.description: Free drag-and-drop Lewis dot structure builder. Practice covalent and ionic bonding, valence electrons and the octet rule with instant checking.
lewis-dot-structures.card: Drag atoms from the periodic table, share or transfer electrons, and check octets for covalent and ionic compounds.
lewis-dot-structures.about: Students drag elements from the periodic table onto a whiteboard and build Lewis dot diagrams by moving actual valence electrons. Two nonmetals share a pair to make a covalent bond, and a metal transfers its electron to a nonmetal to make an ionic bond, so the difference between the two bond types is something students do, not just read.
how: Pick Guided to build assigned compounds, or Free Draw to build your own.
Drag a colored symbol from the periodic table into the build area.
Drag a dot onto another atom to bond. Pull a bond sideways to break it.
Press Check octets, then Save image to keep your structure.
lewis-dot-structures.classroom: Designed for projectors and Smartboards. Use it to model bonding, for partner practice, or for students to save images of their structures for an assignment.

naming-compounds.name: Name ⇄ Formula Trainer
naming-compounds.title: Naming Compounds Practice: Ionic & Covalent Formulas
naming-compounds.description: Free naming compounds practice: write names from formulas and formulas from names for ionic, covalent, transition metal and polyatomic ion compounds.
naming-compounds.card: Practice formula to name and name to formula for ionic, covalent, transition metal and polyatomic compounds.
naming-compounds.about: Nomenclature takes lots of practice, and the first step is deciding whether a compound is ionic or covalent. This trainer has students classify each compound first, then name it or write its formula. Levels build from simple binary compounds to transition metals with Roman numerals and polyatomic ions.
how: Choose Ionic, Covalent or Mixed, then a level from 1 (known charges) to 4 (mixed).
Pick Formula to Name or Name to Formula.
Use the built-in periodic table (blue numbers show group charges) and the Reference list of polyatomic ions.
Check the Score Card to see your progress.
naming-compounds.classroom: Use it as daily nomenclature practice, homework, or test review. The Score Card gives students and teachers a quick progress check.

gas-laws.name: Gas Law Lab
gas-laws.title: Gas Laws Simulation: Boyle's, Charles's & Gay-Lussac's Law Lab
gas-laws.description: Free gas law simulation with a syringe in a water bath. Collect data and graph Boyle's law, Charles's law, Gay-Lussac's law and the combined gas law.
gas-laws.card: A syringe in a water bath: change pressure, volume and temperature, collect data, graph it, and find absolute zero.
gas-laws.about: A virtual syringe in a water bath lets students run real gas law experiments: push or pull the plunger, add weights, or heat and cool the bath, and record pressure, volume and temperature. They graph their own data with a best-fit line, so the relationships in Boyle's, Charles's and Gay-Lussac's laws come from evidence. Extending the line to zero lets them find absolute zero themselves.
how: Pick a law at the top. The green boxes show what is held constant.
Change one variable with the buttons on the model or the Controls box.
Record at least 3 trials (5 or more is better), then graph them. Try P against 1/V for Boyle's law.
Turn on the "constant?" column and answer the challenge questions. Data can be copied to Google Sheets or downloaded as CSV.
gas-laws.classroom: Use it as a full virtual lab, as a pre-lab before a real syringe lab, or to let absent students collect data. Measurement error can be switched on for realistic data.

heating-curve.name: Heating Curve Simulator
heating-curve.title: Heating Curve of Water Simulation: Phase Changes & Energy
heating-curve.description: Free heating and cooling curve of water simulation with real lab footage. See melting, boiling, phase changes, kinetic and potential energy from ice at -50 °C to steam.
heating-curve.card: Heat ice to steam (or cool it back) and watch the graph, the particles and real lab footage stay in sync.
heating-curve.about: Why does the temperature stop rising while ice melts or water boils? This heating curve simulator takes water from ice at -50 °C to steam at 150 °C (or cools it back down) while the graph, the kinetic and potential energy bars, and real time-lapse lab footage of a classroom run play together. The flat parts of the curve become easy to explain: the energy is going into changing the phase, not raising the temperature.
how: Press Play (or the space bar) to run the heating curve. R resets.
Use the arrow keys or the Cooling and Heating buttons to switch direction.
Press V to show or hide the lab view of the real beaker, and F for full screen.
Open Teacher settings to show or hide the graph line, labels and KE/PE bars.
heating-curve.classroom: Project it while teaching phase changes, pause at each segment for students to predict what happens next, or pair it with a real ice-melting lab.

calorimetry.name: Calorimetry & Specific Heat Lab
calorimetry.title: Calorimetry Lab Simulation: Specific Heat & Food Calories
calorimetry.description: Free virtual calorimetry lab. Find the specific heat capacity of metals with q = mcΔT and measure food Calories by burning snacks. Includes real lab videos.
calorimetry.card: Drop hot metal into a calorimeter to find specific heat, burn snack foods to measure Calories, and compare with real lab videos.
calorimetry.about: This virtual calorimetry lab has two parts. In the first, students heat marbles or metal samples and drop them into water to measure the specific heat capacity with q = mcΔT and conservation of energy. In the second, they burn snack foods under a can of water to measure food Calories and compare with the nutrition label. Time-lapse videos of the real class experiments show where real labs lose heat.
how: Follow the glowing hints: blue = drag, yellow = click, green box = drop here, notepad = record it.
Record temperatures in the data table and watch the temperature-time graph and energy bar chart.
Use the Calculations and Questions tabs to solve for heat and specific heat.
Open Real Lab to watch the class experiment videos, and the Reference Table for formulas and specific heat values.
calorimetry.classroom: Use it as a full virtual lab, a pre-lab before the real calorimetry lab, or a make-up lab for absent students.

compounds-vs-molecules.name: Compounds vs Molecules: Classifying Matter
compounds-vs-molecules.title: Compounds vs Molecules: Classifying Matter Interactive Lab & Quiz
compounds-vs-molecules.description: Free interactive lesson on atoms, elements, molecules, compounds, ionic formula units and mixtures, with particle diagrams, a Venn sorter, a build-a-particle lab and a quiz.
compounds-vs-molecules.card: Sort compounds into a Venn diagram, classify particle diagrams as elements, compounds or mixtures, and snap atoms together to build real particles.
compounds-vs-molecules.about: Students learn what atoms, elements, molecules and compounds are, why ionic compounds are compounds but not molecules, and how pure substances differ from homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures. They cut a copper sample down to one atom, watch sodium + chlorine and hydrogen + oxygen react, pull iron out of a mixture with a magnet, then sort compounds into a Venn diagram, classify particle boxes, and snap atoms together to build real substances.
how: Work through the 9 Learn stops (Back/Next or tap a numbered stop).
In the Lab, finish the Venn Sorter (80% or better), the Matter Sorter and Build-a-Particle. Drag items, or tap an item and then a bin.
When the Lab Checklist is done, take the 10-question quiz and download or email your score card.
compounds-vs-molecules.classroom: Use it as interactive notes on classifying matter, as station work, or as review before a quiz on elements, compounds and mixtures. The score card can be turned in through Google Classroom or Gmail.

endothermic-exothermic.name: Endothermic vs Exothermic
endothermic-exothermic.title: Endothermic vs Exothermic Reactions: Hot & Cold Pack Lab, ΔH & Quiz
endothermic-exothermic.description: Free interactive lesson on endothermic and exothermic reactions: system vs surroundings, the sign of ΔH, bond energy, energy diagrams, a hot/cold pack lab and quiz.
endothermic-exothermic.card: Learn ΔH, bond energy and energy diagrams, then dissolve CaCl₂, NaOH, NH₄NO₃ and KCl in a virtual hot pack / cold pack lab.
endothermic-exothermic.about: Students learn the difference between the system and the surroundings, why exothermic reactions have a negative ΔH and endothermic reactions a positive ΔH, how breaking and forming bonds decides the energy change, and how to read potential energy diagrams with activation energy, the activated complex and a catalyst. In the Hot Pack / Cold Pack lab they dissolve CaCl₂, NaOH, NH₄NO₃ and KCl in 100 mL of water, graph temperature against time, classify each process and check the math with q = mcΔT. A scenario sort covers everyday examples and phase changes.
how: Work through the 8 Learn stops (Back/Next or tap a numbered stop).
In Lab A, choose a solid and a mass, then press Drop in & stir. Watch the thermometer and graph, then classify the process and the sign of ΔH.
Test all four solids, then sort the 12 scenario cards in Lab B.
When the Lab Checklist is done, take the 10-question quiz and download, copy or email your score card.
endothermic-exothermic.classroom: Use it as notes and a virtual lab before a real hot pack / cold pack or calorimetry lab, as a make-up lab for absent students, or as review before a thermochemistry quiz. The score card can be turned in through Google Classroom or Gmail.

periodic-trends.name: Periodic Trends
periodic-trends.title: Periodic Trends: Atomic Radius, Ionization Energy, Electron Affinity & Electronegativity
periodic-trends.description: Free interactive periodic trends lesson: atomic radius, ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity with heat maps, atom size comparisons, ranking practice and a quiz.
periodic-trends.card: Explore atomic radius, ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity on interactive heat maps, compare atom sizes and rank elements by trend.
periodic-trends.about: Students learn why the trends happen (nuclear charge, energy levels and shielding), then explore each trend on a main-group periodic table with Period and Group buttons that break out the trend row by row and column by column. The Lab has a full heat-map periodic table with a 3D bar view and trend arrows, a Size Showdown that draws two atoms to scale, and ranking challenges on a colored periodic table. Values: calculated atomic radii (Clementi), NIST/CRC first ionization energies, experimental electron affinities and Pauling electronegativities.
how: Work through the 8 Learn stops (Back/Next or tap a numbered stop). On stops 2–5, tap a Period or Group button to break out the trend.
In Lab A, view all four heat maps; turn on numbers, trend arrows or 3D bars.
In Lab B, tap two elements on the heat map to compare their sizes (3 comparisons).
In Lab C, click the 3 red-circled elements in order from highest to lowest (8 challenges, at least 6 correct).
When the Lab Checklist is done, take the 10-question quiz and download, copy or email your score card.
periodic-trends.classroom: Use it as interactive notes on periodic trends, as a lab day before a trends worksheet, or as review before a periodic table test. The score card can be turned in through Google Classroom or Gmail.

physical-chemical-changes.name: Physical vs Chemical Changes
physical-chemical-changes.title: Physical vs Chemical Properties and Changes: Virtual Lab, Swipe Sort & Quiz
physical-chemical-changes.description: Free interactive lesson on physical and chemical properties and changes: evidence of a chemical change, misleading evidence, a virtual lab bench and a quiz.
physical-chemical-changes.card: Test 11 substances with heat, acid, water, a magnet and fire on a virtual lab bench, spot real vs. fake evidence, and classify physical vs chemical.
physical-chemical-changes.about: Students learn that physical properties (color, state, density, melting and boiling point, hardness, malleability, ductility, conductivity, solubility, magnetism) can be observed without changing a substance, while chemical properties (flammability, reactivity with acid, oxygen or water, rusting and tarnishing) describe its ability to become something new. They compare physical changes with chemical changes, watch atoms rearrange when methane burns, explore the six kinds of evidence of a chemical change and the cases where evidence fools you (boiling bubbles, a cold pack, food coloring, a glowing bulb), then sort tricky cases like the candle. On the Lab Bench they run any of 88 tests on 11 substances (magnesium, ice, an iron nail, sugar, baking soda, a wooden splint, copper wire, salt, steel wool, a candle and chalk), record evidence and classify each result; two 30-card swipe decks sort changes and properties.
how: Work through the 8 Learn stops (Back/Next or tap a numbered stop); each has something to tap or test.

In Lab A, pick a substance and a test (heat, HCl, vinegar, water, crush/cut, magnet, burn or moist air), press Run test, tick the evidence you saw and classify it as a physical change, chemical change or no change.
In Lab B, swipe or drag each card left for Physical or right for Chemical (or use the buttons or arrow keys).
When all Learn stops are viewed and the Lab Checklist is done, take the 10-question quiz and download, copy or email your score card.
physical-chemical-changes.classroom: Use it as notes and a virtual lab before a hands-on physical/chemical change lab, as a make-up lab for absent students (no chemicals needed), or as review before a matter quiz. The Lab Bench works well projected for a whole-class predict-observe-explain. The score card can be turned in through Google Classroom or Gmail.

intermolecular-forces.name: Intermolecular Forces & Polarity
intermolecular-forces.title: Polarity, Intermolecular Forces & Like Dissolves Like: Interactive Chemistry Lesson
intermolecular-forces.description: Free interactive lesson on bond and molecular polarity, London dispersion, dipole–dipole, hydrogen bonding and ion–dipole forces, and like dissolves like, with 3D molecules, virtual labs and a quiz.
intermolecular-forces.card: Find polar bonds from electronegativity, rotate 3D molecules to decide polarity, watch intermolecular forces in a particle microscope and test like dissolves like at a mixing bench.
intermolecular-forces.about: Students learn to find bond polarity from electronegativity (ΔEN cutoffs 0.5 and 1.7, treated as a continuum), show polarity with partial charges, dipole arrows and electron-density maps, and decide molecular polarity from shape. Learn stops compare intramolecular bonds with intermolecular forces, show London dispersion, dipole–dipole, hydrogen bonding and ion–dipole forces with animated particle views and a relative-strength scale, graph the boiling points of the group 14–17 hydrides, and explain like dissolves like with soap micelles, vitamins and dry cleaning. The Lab has a 3D Polarity Explorer with an electric-field box, a charged balloon and liquid stream, an IMF Microscope with a temperature slider and Boiling Race, and a Mixing Bench with water, hexane and ethanol, a two-layer challenge and a soap demo.
how: Work through the 10 Learn stops (Back/Next or tap a numbered stop). Drag the 3D molecules to rotate them.
In Lab A, pick molecules, use the toggles and the electric-field box, then classify 10 molecules as polar or nonpolar and list their IMFs.
In Lab B, choose a liquid, predict, then run the charged-balloon test for 3 liquids.
In Lab C, change the temperature in the IMF Microscope, then run 2 Boiling Races.
In Lab D, test at least 8 solute/solvent combinations and complete the two-layer challenge.
When the Lab Checklist is done, take the 10-question quiz and download, copy or email your score card.
intermolecular-forces.classroom: Use it as interactive notes on polarity and intermolecular forces, as a virtual lab before or after a hands-on solubility or evaporation lab, or as review before a bonding test. The score card can be turned in through Google Classroom or Gmail.
